summary:
Specula is a full pipeline, from NASA's archive to an interactive website, that hunts for moving objects in real photos from the SPHEREx space telescope. NASA releases new SPHEREx photos every week, and Specula is built so each new release can go through the same steps and show what moved.

We gathered 1,401 SPHEREx photos (about 99 GB) of five patches of sky, cleaned them and lined them up. Our detector measured nearly two million bright spots. Stars stay put; asteroids and comets move. So we removed everything that stays still, linked what moves in a straight line, and checked every result against NASA JPL's catalogue.

We tested it on the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. Our pipeline picked it out in 50 photos with zero false alarms, along with Ceres and three known asteroids. No new objects turned up: everything that moved was already known.

On the website, you can scroll through the photos over time, see what moved, and follow each object around the Sun in 3D.

A search for unknown worlds like Planet X only matters if you can trust it. Specula shows the whole search, and exactly how well it works, on real NASA data.
details:
What Specula does

Specula is a full pipeline, from NASA’s archive to an interactive website, that hunts for moving objects in real SPHEREx photos. It downloads the photos, cleans and lines them up, finds every bright spot, throws away the stars, links what moves, and checks every result against NASA JPL. Then it puts the whole search on a website anyone can explore: the photos over time, what moved, and where each object travels around the Sun in 3D.

The data

  • 1,401 SPHEREx photos (May 2025 to August 2026, about 99 GB) from NASA’s IRSA archive.
    • Ecliptic (Virgo) and Ecliptic (RA 90, inside the Milky Way): where asteroids travel.
    • North Ecliptic Pole, home of the Cat’s Eye Nebula: photographed every day, and no known asteroid crosses it, so it tells us how often we’d raise a false alarm.
    • Ceres and 3I/ATLAS: two fields that follow a known object, so we can prove the method works.
  • NASA JPL is our answer key: the position of every known asteroid in every photo, their orbits, and a list of 4,088 known comets.

How it works

  1. Download and verify: every photo is checked against NASA’s own records.
  2. Clean and align: bad pixels are masked, the glow of interplanetary dust is removed, and every photo is lined up on a shared sky grid so each star sits on the same pixel.
  3. Detect: our detector measured every bright spot in every photo, 1,911,543 in total, without seeing any answer data.
  4. Remove the stars: a spot that sits in the same place days apart is a star.
  5. Link what moves: spots that move in a straight line across at least four bursts become a track.
  6. Check: each track is matched to NASA JPL’s catalogue. A match is a known object. Anything left over would be a new candidate, checked against every known comet and given an estimated distance range.

Does it work?

  • We locked our settings before testing on the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.
  • 3I/ATLAS: picked out in 50 photos with zero false points, 2.8″ from NASA’s position.
  • Ceres: found in 134 photos, 0.6″ from NASA’s position.
  • Known asteroids: found in 62% of the photos where they’re brighter than magnitude 15, and 47% between 15 and 17.
  • Noise test: we ran the same steps on scrambled data, where nothing real can move in a straight line, to see how often chance alone would fool us. That test set the bar for a real track.
  • Honest note: our first locked run also kept 39 false paths next to 3I/ATLAS, at the edge of its moving field of view. A stricter rule, chosen only from the scrambled data, removed all of them and kept 3I/ATLAS.
  • No new objects turned up. Everything that moved was already known. That fits what we’d expect: almost every asteroid bright enough for a single SPHEREx photo is already in NASA’s catalogue.

The website

  • Flip through the photos over time, or press Play, in colour composites or single frames.
  • Known objects are circled; click one to see its size range, orbit and how closely we matched NASA.
  • A 3D solar system built from JPL orbits, with SPHEREx’s line of sight drawn in, and a Focus filter that shows only the orbits of what’s in the current photo.
  • A pipeline panel with every score, and an About page listing every data source.
  • Ready for weekly updates: it keeps track of each data release and can mark new photos as NEW.

Benefits and impact

  • NASA releases new SPHEREx photos every week. Specula shows how each release could be searched for things that move, with a score you can trust.
  • Anything new, even a Planet X, would first show up the same way 3I/ATLAS did: as a dot that moves. Specula is built to catch that dot and prove it isn’t a fluke.
  • It turns a research pipeline into something anyone can explore, using real NASA data.

What makes it creative

  • We built the exam in from day one: a real interstellar comet as the test, Ceres as the practice object, and an empty patch of sky to count false alarms.
  • The scrambled-data test measures how often chance alone would fool us, instead of guessing.
  • Search and exploration live in one place: the science numbers sit right next to the photos and the 3D view.

What we considered

  • SPHEREx sees each star in a slightly different colour in each photo, so brightness changes. We judge motion by position, not brightness.
  • NASA publishes photos about six weeks after they’re taken, so the site says “latest published”, not “live”.
  • When IRSA’s cutout service went down, we downloaded full photos and cut our patches ourselves.
  • Honest wording: “recovered”, not “discovered”, and sizes and distances shown as ranges.
  • It works on laptops and phones, with keyboard shortcuts.

Tools

  • Data and detection: Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Astropy, Matplotlib, Pillow).
  • Website: Next.js, React and TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, hosted on Vercel.
  • Data: NASA SPHEREx (IRSA), NASA JPL Small-Body Database, Horizons and sb_ident, and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) and Grok (xAI) were used as AI assistants and helped write parts of our code. Every result was checked by the team against NASA JPL data.

    Code: github.com/MuathLoss/Specula-NASA

Team: Muath Omar Alamoudi (data), Omar Teskyeh (motion detector), Abdullah Zuhair Balila (integration), Reham Ali Abdullah Modhesh (UI design), Amira Ibrahim (frontend support), Mohammed Fuad Abdullah (research and presentation).
